title: 道德經 第三十七章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 37, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 71. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 37 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 為政 (The Conduct of Government). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

morph.gloss: abidingly, as a standing condition — an adverb here, not the noun 'constancy'
acting without forcing — doing nothing that goes against the way a thing is of itself

sentences.l: The Way abidingly acts without forcing
sentences.n: The sense-unit stops in the middle of a sentence because Wang Bi's commentary does: he breaks off here to comment, and this project follows his lemmata rather than inventing divisions of its own, so the thought is finished by the next unit. Textual note, and a large one. Where our received text reads 道常無為, the Mawangdui silk manuscripts read 道恆無名, 'the Way is abidingly nameless' — 恆 being the older word that 常 displaced when 恆 fell under a Han taboo, and 名 'a name' standing where we have 為 'to act'. The Guodian bamboo slips, older still, appear to read 亡為, 'without acting', which is our line in an older spelling. So the two oldest witnesses disagree with each other as well as with us, and the most quoted formula in the chapter may not be the earliest wording.

sentences.l: and yet there is nothing it does not do.
sentences.n: 無不為 is a double negative doing the work of a universal, and it is stronger than 'it does everything' — it goes looking for the exceptions and reports none. The pair of clauses is one of the most quoted sentences in the book, and the contradiction is in the English rather than the Chinese: the 為 denied in 無為 is contrived action pushed against the grain of a thing, while the 為 in 無不為 is simply getting done. Hold the fame of the line lightly, though — the Guodian slips appear to lack this half altogether.

sentences.t:
侯王若能守之，
萬物將自化。
化而欲作，
吾將鎮之以無名之樸。

morph.gloss: lords and kings — the rulers of the day taken together, the men this book keeps addressing
a feudal lord, the ruler of a domain
to guard, to keep, to hold on to
the ten thousand things — every creature and thing there is
of themselves — the reflexive always stands before its verb
to transform, to turn into what they should be
having transformed — the same word again, now the state the next clause starts from
to rise up, to start into action
to press down, to weigh steady — the concrete word for the heavy thing laid on something to keep it still
the uncarved block — timber as it left the tree, before any tool shaped it

sentences.l:
If lords and kings can hold to it,
the ten-thousand things will transform of themselves.
Transformed, and desire rises up:
I will press them steady with the uncarved block that has no name.
sentences.i: If lords and kings could hold to it, the ten thousand things would transform of their own accord; and if, once transformed, desire began to stir, I would weigh them steady with the nameless uncarved block.
sentences.n: 無名之樸 is 'the uncarved block of no-name', and we keep 無 and 名 as two words here, as in chapter 1 — where whether 無名 is one thing at all is the most argued piece of punctuation in the book. 樸 is the single place this project keeps the familiar English: the uncarved block, timber still as it left the tree, is what the Chinese says and nothing better has been found for it. 鎮 is physical before it is political — the paperweight, the stone laid on a thing to stop it shifting — so the ruler of this line does not crush desire but settles it by weight. And watch 自 in 自化: the reflexive stands in front of the verb it belongs to and means 'of itself', not 'itself' as an object. The same shape closes the chapter in 自定, and chapter 25 ended on its most famous instance, 自然, 'so of itself'.

sentences.t:
無名之樸，
夫亦將無欲。

morph.gloss: now — the particle that opens a general observation (fú); read fū it is the noun 'a grown man'

sentences.l:
The uncarved block that has no name —
and they too will be without desire.
sentences.i: The nameless uncarved block: and then they too will want nothing.
sentences.n: The unit opens by repeating the four characters the last one closed with, which is how this book stitches a thought to the next — chapter 16 does it with 歸根曰靜，是謂復命, chapter 25 with its chain of definitions. 夫 here is the small particle that sets a topic up, not the noun 'a man' and not the demonstrative 'that': the reading is fú, and it leaves the sentence with no subject at all. Chapter 32 has the same shape, 夫亦將知止, and gets 'one must also know where to stop'. Who it is that will want nothing is not said; we supply the ten thousand things of the unit before, which is what Wang Bi's 無欲競也 assumes, but the ruler would also stand. Textual note: the Mawangdui manuscripts appear to read 辱 'disgrace' where we have 欲 'desire' — two words that sounded much alike — which turns the line into 'that too will be free of disgrace', and carries the same change through the line that follows.

sentences.t:
不欲以靜，
天下將自定。

morph.gloss: and thereby, and so — 'by that', the that being the not-desiring just named
to settle, to come to rest — settled as a thing set down and no longer shifting

sentences.l:
Not desiring, and thereby still,
all-under-heaven will settle of itself.
sentences.i: Wanting nothing, and so at rest, all under heaven will settle of its own accord.
sentences.n: 以 again with nothing after it — 'by that' — and again the that is the clause just spoken. Notice how little the ruler does in this chapter: his only verb is 守, to hold on, and every other action belongs to the things themselves, which transform, and stir, and settle, 自, of their own accord. A number of editions read 正 zhèng, 'come right', for 定 dìng, 'settle', and the Mawangdui manuscripts appear to read 天地, 'heaven and earth', where we have 天下, 'all under heaven'. Our text prints what stands here.
